metadata.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education: Computer-Assisted Learning and AI-guided Tutors

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This article is a narrative review combined with descriptive and secondary analyses using publicly available PISA 2022 school-level indicators and Google Trends regional search intensity. It does not estimate student-level predictive models from PISA microdata, so there is no requirement to apply PISA sampling weights for an ML estimation stage. For any reuse of PISA 2022 microdata in future empirical work, analysts should apply the OECD/PISA complex survey design weights provided in the OECD data products and follow OECD guidance for variance estimation under the replicate design. The paper’s reported PISA results (e.g., EDUSHORT and digital resource shortage percentages) are taken from OECD tables, which already incorporate the survey design in their published estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the paper does not conduct an ML analysis predicting PISA cognitive achievement PV-based outcomes from student-level microdata. Instead, it synthesizes causal evidence from external CAL/AI tutoring studies and reports secondary PISA 2022 indicators (e.g., principals’ reports of digital resource shortages) and Google Trends search intensity as a proxy for AI adoption. Missing-data handling for PVs is therefore not part of the paper’s estimation workflow.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: No student-level analytic sample is constructed from PISA microdata for ML estimation. The paper uses OECD-published PISA 2022 school questionnaire indicators (e.g., SC017Q09JA and SC017Q10JA) reported at the country level and uses Google Trends regional search intensity for Italy. Therefore, there are no microdata inclusion/exclusion criteria (e.g., grade filters, item completion thresholds, or PV-based outcome construction) specified for an ML pipeline.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 school questionnaire indicators the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Literature synthesis outcome (not student-level prediction), finding that This paper is primarily a review of causal evidence on computer-assisted learning (CAL) and AI-guided tutoring, emphasizing mathematics gains and the importance of pedagogical design (e.g., hint/scaffolding vs. answer-giving). It also provides secondary, non-ML evidence using PISA 2022 school questionnaire indicators on educational and digital resource shortages (EDUSHORT and digital resource lack/quality reported by principals) for OECD countries near Italy, and it reports descriptive regression results on ChatGPT search intensity in Italian regions using Google Trends as a proxy for AI adoption. The paper does not train or evaluate machine learning models on PISA microdata; consequently, there are no PV-based achievement prediction metrics, no ML model comparison, and no survey-weighted ML estimation procedure. The key implication is that equitable adoption depends on digital infrastructure, school capacity, and teacher support, and that unstructured diffusion risks reinforcing existing inequalities. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction is sparse for ML-specific fields because the manuscript is not an empirical predictive ML study on ILSA microdata. It is a review article that synthesizes external causal evaluations and uses secondary OECD PISA 2022 indicators plus Google Trends descriptive/regression evidence, so there is no student-level ML target, no PV-handling workflow, and no reported ML performance metrics.
